title: Merit and giving
hook: at first light, monks walk past with bowls, and lay people fill them

segments.voice: Yesterday, the monk's rule: a long code for monks and nuns, and a short list for everyone else. Your line was five precepts. Which one pinched, and did you keep it till bedtime? Today, what lay people give back. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-three.

First light on a street in a Theravada town. A line of monks comes walking, barefoot, in single file, each holding a covered bowl against the belly. Along the curb, people are already waiting: a grandmother with a pot of rice still steaming, a kid holding a bag of fruit, a man on his way to work with a packet of sticky rice. The monks stop. Lids come off. Spoonfuls go in. Nobody haggles. Nobody pays. The monks don't ask for anything, and in the custom of the round they receive the food quietly and walk on. The odd part, to an outside eye, is who seems grateful. It's the people at the curb. Today's word is what's happening in that bowl.
screen: `FIRST LIGHT. A LINE OF BOWLS.` → `RICE GOES IN. NOBODY PAYS.` → `THE GIVER SEEMS GRATEFUL.`

segments.voice: Dana is the Pali and Sanskrit word for giving. Four turns on it. First, the bowl is a real need. Under the monk's rule we met yesterday, monks don't cook for themselves or store food, so the morning round is how they eat. The texts describe a two-way bargain: lay people give food, robes and shelter, and monks give the teaching. In one short discourse, the Buddha says the two groups support each other, each one helping the other along. Second, merit. Buddhists speak of giving as making merit, a good that comes back to the giver and ripens over time. That's why the person at the curb can be the grateful one. The bowl is an open door, and the monk is the one holding it open. Third, the giver's own heart. In a discourse on the shape of a good gift, the Buddha describes the giver as glad before giving, bright in the mind while giving, and content after giving. The gift isn't finished when the rice leaves the spoon. It runs on in the giver for a while. Fourth, dana isn't only food for monks. Teachers in this tradition talk about giving time, attention, a meal to a neighbor, a kind word. And in the Dhammapada, the Buddha says the gift of the teaching surpasses every other gift. A bowl of rice and a good word belong to the same practice. None of this requires a monk walking past your door. It only requires something to give and someone to receive it.
screen: `THE BOWL IS A REAL NEED.` · `GIVING MAKES MERIT.` · `GLAD BEFORE, DURING AND AFTER.` · `FOOD, TIME, A WORD: ALL DANA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one gift of food. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind someone you'll see today or tomorrow: a coworker, a neighbor, someone in your house, someone on the street. Now picture handing them something to eat. A coffee. Half your lunch. A plate set down without being asked. Stay with the before part, the gladness the discourse talks about, if it shows up. If it doesn't, that's fine too. Just keep the person and the food in mind. The bell holds the time.
Dana. Giving: the food in the monk's bowl, and any gift offered freely, which the Buddha's teaching says gladdens the giver before, during and after. Today's word.
Your line: dana. Today, give food to the person you pictured, and notice three moments: before you hand it over, while you do, and an hour later. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: In Theravada countries, lay Buddhists often place food in monks' bowls on the morning alms round or bring meals to the monastery, and speak of this giving as making merit.

myth: on the alms round, monks ask for the food they want
the monks don't ask. people give, and the monks receive quietly.
Buddhists speak of giving as making merit for the giver
a good that comes back to the giver, which is why the giver can be the grateful one.
in the Dhammapada, the gift of the teaching is called the greatest gift
the Buddha says the gift of the teaching surpasses every other gift.

fork.setup: you're at the curb at first light. a monk stops, and you spoon rice into his bowl. what does he do, by the custom of the round?
options: thanks you warmly and offers a coin back.
asks for more rice for the monastery.
receives it quietly and walks on.
fork.reveal: he receives it quietly and walks on. in the tradition's way of seeing it, the chance to give is itself the gift, so the giver is the grateful one.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali dāna: giving, generosity.

trapdoor: what you thought: monks begging for food.
what it means: dana, giving freely, in a two-way bond: lay people give food, monks give the teaching.
what a scholar hears: puñña, merit. the discourses describe the giver glad before, during and after, so the gift ripens in the one who gives.

sources.ref: Itivuttaka 107 (monks and householders support each other)

notes: Monks receiving 'quietly' without thanks: custom varies by country and community (some chant a blessing, anumodana). Confirm the phrasing 'in the custom of the round'.
Itivuttaka 107 cited for mutual support between monks and householders; confirm the reference.
AN 6.37 cited for the giver glad before, bright-minded during, content after; confirm reference and paraphrase.
Dhammapada 354 paraphrased (gift of the Dhamma surpasses all gifts); Max Müller wording not quoted.
Vinaya rules forbidding monks to cook or store food are simplified; confirm.
The practice uses 'picture handing them something' inside the practice (not the hook); outline practice 'give food to someone' moved to the carry.
